summary: AI-driven software-intensive embedded systems (SIES) depend on data during development and operation. Poor data quality (DQ) may weaken data trustworthiness, yet evidence about its effects and lifecycle management remains fragmented. This systematic literature review synthesizes 27 primary studies published from January 2020 to February 2026. It examines DQ concerns and evidence linking them to reduced data trustworthiness, along with assessment and management methods. The review identifies 16 concerns organized as Source Quality and Content Quality. Studies provide DQ-based scores and evidence of effects on model or decision performance. Synthesis suggests upstream source or handling problems may become embedded in training baselines and remain difficult to detect at runtime. Eight method categories were identified. Runtime monitoring is the largest category, while upstream and training-time controls remain poorly integrated with runtime assurance. No study covers the full lifecycle. Data trustworthiness supports reliable SIES decisions but is one component of AI-system trustworthiness.

title: A Dynamic Model and Stability Analysis of a Grid-Interactive Data Center
summary: The rapid growth of data centers is creating new interactions between computational workload and power-system dynamics, with potentially significant implications for grid stability. We develop a four-dimensional nonlinear dynamical model of a data center campus interconnected with the bulk power system through a modified Single Machine Infinite Bus system. The model couples generator swing dynamics with a fluid-limit model of computational workload backlog and a grid-interactive data center power controller that incorporates both frequency feedback and computational backpressure. This formulation captures the coupled evolution of generator frequency, rotor angle, computational workload, and data center power consumption, providing a framework for studying the stability implications of flexible data center operation.

title: Berry Esseen bounds for fractional Vasicek type processes: continuous and high-frequency regimes
summary: We study the estimation of the drift parameters $(a,b)$ of the fractional Vasicek process $dX_t=a(b-X_t)\,dt+dB^H_t$, driven by a fractional Brownian motion of Hurst index $H\in(0,1)$. The estimators are of moment type, built from the empirical mean and variance of the path, and are analysed in two regimes: continuous observation on $[0,T]$, and high-frequency observation at times $t_i=iΔ_n$ with $Δ_n\to0$ and $T_n=nΔ_n\to\infty$. Using the Malliavin--Stein method on the second Wiener chaos, we prove consistency of both estimators for every $H$, and quantitative central limit theorems in the Wasserstein distance: for $H<\frac34$ for the estimator of $a$, with explicit rates depending on $H$, and for every $H\in(0,1)$ for the estimator of $b$, at the rate $T^{-H}$. In the discrete regime the bounds contain an additional discretization term of order $Δ_n^{\min\{H+1/2,\,1\}}$, and for $H<\frac12$ the central limit theorem for the estimator of $b$ requires in addition $T_n^{1-2H}Δ_n^{1+2H}\to0$. A short Monte Carlo study illustrates the results.

title: Measuring What Matters in the Age of AI: The Research Software Metrics Landscape
summary: Research software now serves as a primary instrument of science, but the methods the community uses to judge its quality, sustainability, reuse, and impact remain scattered across software engineering, open science, FAIR software, citation, and research-assessment literature. AI-assisted development sharpens the problem: code can be produced at rates that outpace human review capacity, provenance and attribution are harder to track, scholarly credit systems cannot keep pace, and existing metrics inherit assumptions about how research software gets developed that may no longer apply. To aid in navigating these challenges, we present a focused landscape synthesis of research software metrics based on 49 substantive references, organizing the recurring metrics into eight families described by data source, claimed construct, evidence of validity, automation potential, and susceptibility to misuse. Many widely cited research software metrics serve as partial signals but make weak standalone measures of scientific impact. The AI era opens or widens gaps around provenance, maintainability of generated code, reviewer effort, model and data dependencies, reuse and community-health signal inflation, and credit for human labor that AI does not perform. We argue for responsible, contextual, mixed-method use of research software metrics, and offer decision guidance for Research Software Engineers (RSEs), principal investigators, institutions, and funders selecting metrics that support better software, fairer credit, and more trustworthy science. All findings rest on the 49-reference focused review; a reproducible search-and-triage protocol and a 727-record triaged corpus accompany the paper as a transparency artifact for a future full systematic mapping study.

title: Rented Oscillations: Multi-Tenant Data Center Workload Synchronization Attacks and Mitigation
summary: Multi-tenant data center (DC) facilities rent computing capacity on demand, placing controllable load within reach of anyone willing to pay for it. This paper considers a stealthy adversary who rents workstations and runs deliberately unoptimized large language model (LLM) training, synchronizing their consumption into large periodic oscillations while each workload remains individually indistinguishable from benign training. The periodicity of such workloads is characterized experimentally and used to model facility consumption, showing that oscillations emerge from the interaction of concurrent workloads, whether aligned by an adversary or arising naturally. A combined small- and large-signal assessment, under a hardware-grounded threat model whose feasibility is supported by experiments on a supercomputer, locates the oscillatory weak points of the network. MW-scale oscillations are shown to saturate the generators' control limiters, amplifying their effect, while Floquet analysis reveals a lightly damped mode emerging near the forcing frequency. To counter both origins, signal-energy-based detection and mitigation are proposed, the latter re-timing the workloads to minimize the facility's oscillatory energy. The approach is validated through power hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) experiments and real-time simulations on a surrogate model of the Saudi Arabian transmission network.

title: ReliFlow: Reliability-Calibrated Residual Transport for Combinatorial Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
summary: Predicting the transcriptional response to combined perturbations requires distinguishing interactions between interventions from errors in their individual effect estimates. The latter become more pronounced when single-perturbation evidence is sparse or withheld. We introduce a conditional flow-matching model that estimates the reliability of single-gene effects from training-only cross-fitting and uses those estimates to calibrate the additive source distribution. The velocity is decomposed into a known correction of the additive reference and a learned residual transport field. On Norman genetic perturbations, reduces mean absolute error (MAE) from 0.142 to 0.131 for unseen combinations of observed singles and from 0.198 to 0.178 when constituent singles are withheld. On held-out ComboSciPlex drug combinations, MAE decreases from 0.191 to 0.176. Non-additive residual correlation improves from 0.574 to 0.638, and component ablations identify the contribution of reliability weighting. The results indicate that accounting for uncertain constituent effects improves generalization to unseen genetic and chemical combinations, with a moderate increase in training cost.

title: Structure-Behavior Coalescence: A Definition of Systems
summary: For more than seventy years, systems engineering has developed extensive models and frameworks, yet the fundamental question of what constitutes a system remains insufficiently formalized. Existing approaches often treat structure and behavior as separate aspects, leaving their unity, system identity, and consistency conditions insufficiently defined. This paper introduces Structure-Behavior Coalescence (SBC) as a formal framework that defines a system as an integrated entity in which structure and behavior are coalesced through interaction. SBC provides a formal modeling approach with well-formedness constraints for maintaining structural-behavioral coherence, including representations for terminal, paused, and intermediate states and rules for sequential, parallel, and alternative behaviors. The framework provides a formal perspective on the question, "What is a system?", and establishes a foundation for consistent system modeling, verification, and analysis.

title: Fisher Information Characterization in GNSS DPE under Multipath-Induced Channel Uncertainty
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: The availability and utilization of Fisher information in global navigation satellite system (GNSS) direct position estimation (DPE) under multipath-induced channel uncertainty are investigated. First, a unified estimation-theoretic framework is developed to characterize information mapping and utilization across direct and two-step receivers. Next, a scalar-equivalent statistical channel model for short-delay multipath is established via least-squares (LS) projection. Based on this model, receiver-state Cramér-Rao bounds (CRBs) are derived under perfect and statistical channel knowledge, while misspecified CRBs (MCRBs) are derived under a simplified deterministic complex-gain model that neglects channel uncertainty. The closed-form approximations and asymptotic analyses of the derived bounds further reveal how channel uncertainty affects different components of waveform-domain Fisher information. Our results reveal that: 1) DPE and fully coupled two-step estimation achieve comparable accuracy, whereas the performance loss caused by sequential decoupling substantially exceeds the additional loss from suboptimal weighting; 2) under statistical channel knowledge, improving received signal quality does not necessarily yield noticeable positioning gains; 3) positioning information remains available even as the coherent channel mean vanishes; and 4) neglecting channel randomness causes the MCRBs to diverge in this limit and can introduce positioning error floors that become more pronounced with longer observations.

title: How Reward Gain Imbalance Shapes Ranking: Rethinking Rubric-Based Reward Aggregation
summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning constructs rewards for aligning large language models with human preferences, typically by equally aggregating continuous scores that a judge assigns to individual criteria. However, scoring heterogeneity across criteria can distort candidate rankings. Existing work has focused on improving judges, learning criterion weights, or refining aggregation, whereas the interaction between scoring heterogeneity and ranking remains insufficiently understood. We formalize this heterogeneity as \emph{reward gain imbalance}: each criterion enters the aggregated reward with its own reward gain, the gap between its expected scores on satisfied and unsatisfied responses. Counterintuitively, our experiments show that removing this imbalance, even with ground-truth labels, lowers ranking accuracy. To explain this, we derive an exact decomposition of the reward difference between any two candidates into a base satisfaction signal, a reward gain imbalance term, and a residual term, showing that reward gain imbalance can attenuate or amplify the base signal, and finding that misrankings usually concentrate on pairs where it attenuates. Guided by this analysis, we propose the adaptive \textbf{D}ual-\textbf{C}enter \textbf{C}lipping aggregation (DCC), which bounds each criterion's contribution to the reward difference instead of simply removing the imbalance. Using only the scores of the current candidate group, it determines a clipping interval that imposes a common upper bound on per-criterion score differences between candidates, limiting the excessive influence of extreme scores while preserving continuous judgment information....

title: Structure-Behavior Coalescence for Model-Based Systems Engineering
summary: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has advanced system design and analysis for decades, yet traditional approaches often treat structure and behavior separately, resulting in inconsistencies, incomplete models, and ambiguity. This paper introduces Structure-Behavior Coalescence (SBC) as a formal and unified definition of systems for MBSE. SBC defines a system as a single integrated entity in which structure and behavior are coalesced through interaction, providing both a conceptual foundation and a formal process-algebra framework. Well-formedness constraints ensure that interactions are structurally grounded and compositions are valid, enabling consistency by construction. Boundary processes, including 0 for terminal states and a checkpoint construct for paused or suspended states, allow inactive and intermediate states to be represented while preserving system unity. Illustrative examples and a Smart Healthcare IoT case study demonstrate how SBC supports sequential, parallel, and alternative behaviors while maintaining structural-behavioral coherence. SBC provides a foundation for formal verification, compositional modeling, and systematic inconsistency detection, connecting a rigorous definition of systems with practical MBSE applications.

title: Towards Environment-Aware 6G Network Planning: An Any-to-Any Channel Knowledge Map Approach
summary: Planning sixth-generation (6G) networks for reliable coverage across diverse environments is challenging, as it requires channel knowledge between candidate network node locations and potential service regions. This article proposes an environment-aware network planning framework based on any-to-any (X2X) channel knowledge maps (CKMs), which characterize channels between arbitrary transmitter-receiver location pairs. Within this framework, we first construct X2X CKMs from environmental information, sparse channel measurements, or both, with map types and spatial resolutions selected according to the planning task. We then use these maps to predict coverage and optimize network deployment and configuration subject to service requirements and practical constraints, while accounting for subsequent network operation. Finally, field measurements assess channel prediction accuracy and deployment performance, providing feedback for CKM correction and deployment refinement. We discuss implementation methods and tradeoffs across these stages. Case studies illustrate the effectiveness of the framework for indoor intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) deployment and outdoor base station (BS) deployment. Live-network trials further demonstrate coverage gains from IRS deployment and BS reconfiguration, with measurement feedback supporting CKM calibration and configuration refinement.

title: NOTREKS: Marginal Independence in Score-based Structure Learning
summary: Score-based structure learning estimates causal graphs by optimizing a data-dependent objective over structural equation models. We study how prior knowledge that selected pairs of variables are marginally independent can be incorporated into such causal discovery methods. Under faithfulness, marginally independent pairs cannot be connected by a trek, so the knowledge becomes a graphical no-trek constraint, which we call NOTREKS information. We introduce a power-series trek (PSTrek) penalty for gradient-based optimization and a trek constraint for order-based search, and we analyze why such information helps in finite samples and how it restricts the search space. Our numerical experiments illustrate to what extent NOTREKS information helps in causal discovery. In particular, using synthetic benchmarks with oracle NOTREKS information, we show that these constraints can improve both structural recovery and adjustment-based effect identification.

title: Generative AI in Software Testing: Practitioners' Perspectives on the Benefits, Challenges, Opportunities, and Risks
comment: Accepted for publication in 27th International Conference on Product-Focused Software Process Improvement (PROFES 2026)
summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) increasingly supports software testing, yet empirical evidence on practitioners' perceptions remains limited. This study investigates perceived benefits, challenges, opportunities, and risks of GenAI in software testing through a questionnaire survey of 64 practitioners. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively, while open-ended responses were qualitatively coded to contextualize the findings. Among the respondents, 34 were users (those with regular or experimental use of GenAI in testing) and 30 were non-users (those without prior use of GenAI in testing). Results show generally positive perceptions of GenAI for reducing effort, test generation, and debugging, alongside concerns about prompt dependence, trust, and incorrect outputs. Users were more positive about several concrete benefits while also more frequently prioritizing reliability-related risks, whereas non-users showed greater uncertainty about some technically specific challenges. Overall, the findings position GenAI as an assistive technology requiring human validation and highlight the importance of considering practitioners' experience with GenAI when interpreting perceptions of GenAI-assisted testing.

title: Beyond Intelligibility: Fine-Grained Perceptual Assessment of Dysarthric Speech with Auditory Large Language Models
comment: 5 pages; Haotian Wei, Can Long, and Wen Xian Jim contributed equally
summary: Accurate assessment of dysarthric speech is vital for clinical diagnosis and rehabilitation, yet existing automated methods rely heavily on isolated, single-task models or generic speech quality metrics that fail to disentangle heterogeneous neuromotor deficits. This work presents the first systematic investigation into adapting auditory large language models (ALLMs) for multi-dimensional dysarthric speech assessment under a unified, prompt-conditioned framework. Four representative ALLMs are benchmarked across five clinical perceptual dimensions from the Speech Accessibility Project (SAP): naturalness, monopitch, intelligibility, imprecise consonants, and inappropriate silences. To bridge generic perceptual quality and clinical evaluation, a two-stage training paradigm is explored, leveraging out-of-domain pre-training followed by in-domain clinical adaptation. Experimental results demonstrate that leading ALLMs reliably capture fine-grained pathological variations, exhibiting distinct and complementary strengths across prosodic and articulatory attributes. These findings establish ALLMs as a scalable foundation for clinical speech evaluation and provide practical insights into model selection and multi-task transfer potential.

title: Is It Worth Collecting Additional Covariates?
summary: In many studies, basic covariates are routinely recorded at negligible cost, whereas acquiring additional covariates requires expensive or time-consuming procedures. Thus, a natural question is whether it is worth to collecting these additional covariates. Using the reduction in prediction interval width as criterion, we evaluate and test the gain brought by the additional covariates and hence answer this question. We consider the gain both marginally and conditionally on the observable characteristics. The conditional formulation captures subpopulation heterogeneity and supports individualized data acquisition decisions. To avoid restrictive parametric assumptions, we adopt a model-free framework that accommodates flexible nonparametric or machine learning methods. We propose an efficient influence function based method, with proven theoretical properties to achieve our purpose under mild nuisance convergence rates. Interestingly, we find the natural conformal prediction based method cannot achieve the same purpose: It fails in the marginal case and imposes much more stringent or even infeasible requirement on the nuisance parameter estimation procedures. We demonstrate the superior finite-sample performance of the proposed procedures through simulations and real data applications.

title: StatePortal: Agentic Checkpoint Synthesis for Testing Deep States in Interactive Software
summary: Large language models have reduced the effort to generate code for interactive software with graphical user interfaces (GUIs). For such software, a key testing bottleneck is reaching a deep state, one that requires a long interaction history. The cost of reaching it recurs across commits, and the GUI automation that could amortize it assumes a DOM or accessibility tree that self-rendered engines do not expose. We introduce StatePortal, an agent that synthesizes a checkpoint, an artifact that restores that state and can be versioned and replayed, from a natural-language functional test case and read-only access to the target's source code. The checkpoint is restored through a per-application hook that an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes once without hand-written hook code. Because a checkpoint can satisfy state checks while rendering incorrectly, checkpoints are scored by hybrid programmatic-state and visual evaluation: acceptance requires both a programmatic-state oracle and a visual oracle to pass. We calibrate the visual oracle against a blinded cross-VLM reference. We release DeepStateBench, 61 deep-state tasks across 10 interactive applications that span five language families and six rendering stacks, with source sizes from 874 to 7.2M lines. Across three registered models, a GUI agent seeded with synthesized checkpoints completes 10.4% of trials, compared with 0% without seeding under the same pixel action space, while StatePortal, which also delivers the target action through the hook, completes 27.5%. Over 1,361 replays of 112 checkpoints, 98.90% reproduce the original verdict with zero model calls, and the hybrid oracle detects 96.25% (77/80) of controlled visual faults invisible to programmatic-state checks alone. We open-source our code at https://github.com/pzy2000/State_Portal and website at https://stateportal.mineyosemite.chatgpt.site

title: Mitigating the Grid Impact of Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers via High-Fidelity Model Flexibility
summary: Gigawatt-scale artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) are being connected at a single point of interconnection (POI) faster than transmission can be reinforced, yet studies of their flexibility rely on DC power flow and simplified load envelopes that omit voltage, cooling dynamics, and workload deadlines. This paper addresses this gap by embedding a high-fidelity AIDC model, with separate inference and training pools, hall thermal mass, PV, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with reactive capability, and a STATCOM, in a five-minute multi-period AC optimal power flow. Simulations on the RTS-GMLC test system show that active-power flexibility mitigates local price spikes and relieves congestion, whereas reactive support from the BESS inverter or a STATCOM is needed to keep the POI voltage away from sagging around its 0.95~pu limit. Sensitivity analyses show that cost-driven charging of large batteries can induce new morning congestion and that storage largely substitutes for wider workload deferral.

title: Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Causal Function Recovery under Network Interference
summary: Causal inference seeks to learn how outcomes change under alternative interventions, but network interactions complicate this task. Under network interference, outcomes depend on both own treatment and neighbors' treatments, making causal effects functions of neighborhood exposure rather than single treatment contrasts. Existing methods primarily target prespecified causal contrasts or their estimation precision, leaving global response-function recovery largely unexplored. We study sequential experimentation under a limited experimental budget, with the goal of recovering the full exposure-dependent population-average response function. To this end, we propose FANCI (Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Network-Interference Causal Inference). For function learning, treatment-specific Gaussian processes flexibly model nonlinear conditional response surfaces. For experimental design, we formulate global response-function recovery as a coverage problem and propose a fill-distance criterion that guides new experiments toward poorly covered regions. To account for network constraints on attainable exposure patterns, we develop full-network and target-screened strategies for selecting feasible network--assignment pairs. Theoretically, we derive uniform error bounds linking fill distance to response-function estimation and characterize the approximation loss from target screening. Simulations and an online-game experiment show that FANCI improves recovery of nonlinear exposure-dependent effects and reveals treatment patterns obscured when network interference is ignored.

title: EnvAgent: Multi-Agent Approach to Building Science Environments in the Clouds
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at AI4S@SC26 (SC26 Workshop)
summary: AI agents are transforming scientific computing and software workflows, but generating and executing code requires a correctly configured execution environment. Automating environment construction remains difficult because repositories encode heterogeneous, often incomplete requirements for operating systems, toolchains, dependencies, and build procedures. Existing workflows thus rely on developer-maintained Dockerfiles and setup scripts, making preparation labor-intensive, hard to scale, and potentially biasing evaluations. We present ENVAGENT, an agentic framework that synthesizes, builds, and verifies repository-level Docker environments. ENVAGENT combines deterministic utilities for Docker execution and state management with coordinated agents for repository analysis, planning, Dockerfile synthesis, and iterative failure diagnosis and repair. We also introduce ENVBENCH, a benchmark of 54 scientific artifacts and open-source repositories spanning seven languages from Chameleon Trovi and Multi-SWE-bench. For each repository, we curate a declarative rubric of required structure, configuration, and functionality, and a shared evaluator applies 2,108 weighted checks across generated environments. Across four matched language-model settings, ENVAGENT constructs 43.5 executable environments out of 54 on average, versus 23.5 for Codex and Claude Code, and scores 62.02 versus 24.19 on a composite of executability and rubric satisfaction. These results show that environment-specific agent orchestration substantially improves automated environment construction.

title: Approximating Anisotropic Solar Radiation Pressure
comment: 33 pages, 21 figures, 4 tables. Accepted manuscript of the article published in Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics
summary: Solar radiation pressure (SRP) significantly influences satellite dynamics in high-altitude orbits, depending not only on the satellite's trajectory and attitude but also on its surface optical characteristics. Metallic surfaces, such as solar cells with periodic metal bars, exhibit anisotropic reflection that produces an anisotropic SRP. The difficulty in dealing with anisotropic SRP arises because anisotropic SRP does not have a general analytical solution, and accurate computation therefore requires numerical integration. An analytical formulation of anisotropic SRP is useful for stability analysis and controller design for satellites that exploit SRP. To this end, this paper derives an analytical approximation method to calculate the anisotropic SRP modeled with the Ashikhmin-Shirley model. The anisotropy is approximated using multiple spherical Gaussians. Because the product of spherical Gaussians is also a spherical Gaussian, anisotropic reflection can be expressed in an analytically tractable form. The approximation accuracy of the anisotropic SRP is numerically verified for two cases: weak anisotropy and strong anisotropy.

title: A probabilistic analysis of the Brumadinho tailings dam-breach using uncertainty quantification and global sensitivity analysis
summary: On 25th January 2019, Dam B1 in Brumadinho, Brazil, suddenly collapsed and produced a catastrophic tailings flow with severe human, environmental and infrastructural consequences. Previous numerical back-analyses of the tailings flow have relied on deterministic approaches, which provide useful reference results but do not explicitly incorporate uncertainty associated to rupture hydrograph and tailings' physical properties. This work presents a probabilistic approach to study the tailings dam-breach flow caused by the rupture of Dam B1, focusing on the quantification and interpretation of the effects of input uncertainty on hazard-related hydrodynamical outputs. Deterministic data was obtained through HEC-RAS v6.6 by considering tailings as an one-phase Bingham fluid. The probabilistic framework combines dimensionality reduction, metamodeling and flooding classification to perform fast prediction of unexplored input scenarios. It allows to obtain data distributions that reflect output uncertainty and to estimate variance-based sensitivity indices to quantify the influence of input uncertainty over output variability. Results show that uncertainty is strongly dependent on time and spatial location. Hydrograph-related parameters mainly control the timing and magnitude of the early flow, whereas yield stress becomes more influential in regions associated with flow attenuation, spreading and possible arrest. Overall, the framework provides probabilistic hazard estimates and insights into the physical mechanisms governing the dynamics of tailings flow.

title: Controlled Natural Language for Requirements Specification: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Requirements are critical artifacts of the software development life-cycle. They express capabilities that the system should provide, guiding both the development and testing process. Given their significance, require- ments specification has attracted the interest of researchers and practitioners in recent years. Requirements specification is an activity where requirements are specified, i.e., documented. In this context, Controlled Natural Languages (CNL) were proposed as a compromise between the ambiguity of natural language and the complexity of formal languages. CNLs enable the specification of requirements using accurate statements that can be processed automatically, while remaining understandable by stakeholders. In this article, we perform a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to identify, categorize, and compare CNL approaches for requirements specification. The SLR covers 133 primary studies published between 2000 and 2024. We evaluate them accord- ing to seven dimensions: context, scope, targeted requirements types, specification technique, tool support, validation method, and adoption. We provide a categorization framework that summarizes the evaluated dimensions, and we identify directions for future research. Our main results reveal: (1) four types of CNL: standalone templates, requirement patterns, elementary templates, and linguistic rules, (2) limited support for automated tools and domain vocabulary usage, and (3) lack of validation through case studies and limited adoption for the majority of approaches.

title: Control-Aware Separating Hyperplanes for Control Barrier Functions in Planar Navigation
summary: Separating hyperplanes are widely used in Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based collision avoidance, yet their orientations strongly govern control intervention-the deviation of the applied control from the robot's nominal command. Existing methods typically select hyperplane orientations from geometry alone. Jointly optimizing orientations and control yields a continuous, non-convex problem in which local nonlinear solvers suffer from initialization sensitivity, local minima, and unpredictable latency, while discretized orientation grids scale exponentially with obstacle count. For planar navigation of a polygonal robot among polygonal obstacles, we present a solver-free, control-aware separating hyperplane selection method that directly computes a global optimum of this joint problem at each step whenever it is feasible. Exploiting the geometry of Minkowski difference polygons, we reduce this continuous non-convex optimization to evaluating a polynomial-size set of candidate control interventions via closed-form algebraic checks, selecting the feasible candidate of minimum norm. Across 250 simulated navigation scenarios, our method reduces cumulative intervention cost by 3.6% at the median and 27.3% at the 90th percentile compared to a local nonlinear solver, and completion time by 0.6% and 5.6%, respectively. In scalability benchmarks, it achieves a 6.1x per-step speedup at 16 simultaneous obstacles.

title: Rare-Tail Statistics For Learning Biased Gaussian Halfspaces with Label Noise
summary: We revisit the classical problem of learning general Gaussian halfspaces in the presence of label noise, with particular focus on the large-bias regime, where information-computation gaps are conjectured in several standard label-noise models. Concretely, we present and analyze the rare-tail mean estimator, an extremely simple one-shot statistic that averages only the observed minority class. In the large-bias regime, classical Averaging (Servedio, 1999) and related global first-moment statistics are provably suboptimal, while the rare-tail mean estimator recovers the target halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate (modulo log factors) under a broad class of label noise models, including probit noise and margin-dependent noise with very slow decay away from the boundary. Notably, our guarantees allow labels arbitrarily close to the decision boundary to be nearly random, while still giving strong directional recovery from a small number of samples. The estimator also cleanly interpolates between the noiseless and noisy regimes: without noise, it attains the same sample rate as classical separability-based methods for realizable halfspaces, and under low noise, or noise that decays away from the boundary, it keeps this rate even after linear separability has been destroyed. As an application, we consider a two-stage curriculum in which source samples, whose noise may be arbitrarily close to $1/2$ near the boundary and decay very slowly away from it, precede target samples, whose noise flips every label at the same rate, i.e., random classification noise (RCN). Since both stages share the same Bayes optimal halfspace, our estimator supplies the directional warm start needed by existing refinement routines, and together they learn the RCN target at the information-theoretic sample rate in the large-bias regime, up to log factors.

title: Software Engineering for LLM-Based Agents: A Lifecycle-Oriented Survey
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based Agents perform tasks through tool use and interaction with external environments. Public engineering guidance commonly begins with a target task, selects a suitable workflow or autonomous Agent design, and refines prompts, tools, and execution strategies using task outcomes, latency, and cost. When delivered as software systems, Agents must also satisfy stakeholder requirements, action boundaries, quality checks, and maintenance needs. Model-directed execution can vary across runs, failures can span model decisions and tools, and changes to prompts, models, or interfaces can affect previously accepted behavior. This survey examines how LLM-based Agents are engineered across five software lifecycle stages: Requirements Engineering, Architecture and Design, Implementation and Integration, Testing and Assurance, and Maintenance and Evolution. Based on a main collection of 355 papers, we compare the engineering problems addressed, explain how methods and practices work, and examine their reported evaluations and limitations within each stage. We synthesize how existing research supports Agent development activities and identify open problems and research directions. The result is a lifecycle-oriented reference for understanding, selecting, and further developing methods for engineering Agent software.

title: Trade-off Between Airspace and Channel Capacity for Low-altitude Wireless Network
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures; submitted to IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems (TAES)
summary: Communication-serviceable capacity for low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) networks depends on both spatial occupancy and wireless quality of service (QoS). This paper formulates a communication-feasible occupancy-planning model that maps candidate-grid assignments to concurrent beam loads and per-user rates under fixed-stream and fixed-beam power. With fixed effective noise, per-beam QoS screening determines maximum admission, and an exact dynamic program maximizes aggregate spectral efficiency at that fixed admission. Signal-level simulations validate the SINR expressions, while an explicit-array model examines load-dependent inter-beam leakage. The dynamic program is globally optimal for the separable integer problem, but that guarantee does not extend to the coupled problem. Equal-time orthogonal multiple access (OMA) and ideal-SIC non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) are evaluated through the same local beam reduction under fixed effective noise and fixed per-beam power.

title: DOA Estimation in Antenna Arrays: Super-Resolution Methods in a Common Space
summary: This paper introduces a unified framework for angular super-resolution in antenna arrays. By integrating linear prediction beyond the physical aperture, entropy variations, and harmonic spatial spectra averaging, we recast classical methods - including Capon, Pisarenko, Maximum Entropy, and MUSIC - into a single structure. We extend this framework to accommodate ESPRIT-type methods by treating the number of simultaneously predicted subarray channels as an additional dimension. Furthermore, we adapt this approach to non-Gaussian signals, establishing a parallel framework for Virtual-ESPRIT-type methods. As a practical application, we propose universal, J-orthogonalization-based algorithms that estimate spatial super- resolution spectra within a unified computational architecture. This architecture produces spatial spectrum estimates for multiple super-resolution methods and any intermediate variations.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Finance and the Early-Career Skills Shift: A Structured Evidence Synthesis of Decision Delegation, Bank Deployments, and Business Education
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Structured evidence synthesis of AI in finance, decision delegation, early-career work, and business education. No new experimental measurements are claimed; empirical findings and deployment claims are attributed to cited sources
summary: Artificial intelligence is becoming a general interaction and decision-support layer across finance. Banks use AI for research retrieval, document synthesis, meeting follow-up, customer service, coding, fraud detection, risk support, and increasingly multi-step workflows. This paper asks which parts of finance work can be delegated safely, which remain human-owned, and how education should change when AI compresses the tasks through which novices traditionally build judgment. It presents a structured evidence synthesis of research and public evidence released from 2023 through October 2026 across finance, labor economics, education, bank deployments, and financial regulation. Numerical results and deployment claims remain attributed to their original sources. Four connections emerge: AI is strongest at retrieval, transformation, coding, and first-pass analysis; financial institutions are moving toward constrained rather than unrestricted autonomy; productivity assistance can weaken apprenticeship when assisted output improves faster than unaided capability; and delegation should depend jointly on consequence, reversibility, verification strength, and operational resilience. The paper develops a Finance Work Stack, Decision Delegation Matrix, AI Apprenticeship Paradox, Apprenticeship Preservation Protocol, and Career Readiness Stack. It argues that useful financial AI must improve productivity without weakening accountability, human capability, cyber resilience, or the future talent pipeline.

title: Physical Layer Security for Digital Semantic Communication: A Bit-Level Perspective
summary: Digital semantic communication requires reliable recovery of task-relevant information at a legitimate receiver while limiting source reconstruction by an eavesdropper. Uniform bit protection, however, does not account for the heterogeneous reliability and secrecy requirements of semantic bits. This paper proposes a bit-level physical layer security (PLS) framework that learns these requirements and incorporates them into physical-layer resource allocation. We first introduce a wiretap semantic feature channel whose two-stage training learns per-bit target bit-flip probabilities for the legitimate receiver (Bob) and the eavesdropper (Eve). These targets characterize the reliability requirements at Bob and the secrecy protection requirements against Eve. Based on the learned targets, we formulate a joint power and artificial-noise (AN) allocation problem for a multiple-input single-output wiretap channel under a worst-case angular-separation model. For a given target profile, the optimal information-AN power split admits a closed-form solution, and the per-bit power allocation is obtained by water-filling. We further develop a leakage-aware selection method among multiple learned-target profiles and extend the design to multiple-input multiple-output channels. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a better trade-off between preserving reconstruction quality at Bob and degrading that at Eve than uniform power allocation and the evaluated learning-based secure semantic communication schemes.

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond
summary: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) plays a central role as a dimension-reduction and representation tool in functional data analysis, but its minimax theory for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observation has remained open for over two decades. To fill this gap, we consider a sieve-based FPCA framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects and accommodates sampling frequencies ranging from sparse to dense under random designs. We begin by establishing new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes beyond tensor-product low-complexity structures, thereby identifying the intrinsically two-dimensional optimal rate. Our central theoretical contribution is to establish minimax optimal rates for both individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimensions, under explicit growth and regularity conditions. To establish these results, we develop a general framework for sharp minimax analysis of FPCA under discrete observation, separating spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations and exploiting their distinct structures, thereby offering a new approach to a broad class of nonparametric spectral estimation problems. For both spectral targets, the optimal rates reveal two distinct statistical mechanisms, spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction, whose interplay gives rise to either four or two sampling regimes. This yields, for the first time, a precise characterization of the impact of discrete sampling across the full range from sparse to dense designs. Finally, as a downstream application, we analyze FPCA-based functional linear regression and show that the FPCA-based estimator attains the minimax-optimal rates.

title: Perceived Effectiveness of Social Debt Mitigation Measures: A Preliminary Vignette-Based Survey
summary: Software engineering is a socio-technical discipline in which unresolved social and organizational problems accumulate as social debt, gradually eroding collaboration and project health. The literature offers a solid vocabulary for these problems but says little about which countermeasures practitioners consider effective. We address this gap with a vignette-based survey: six social debt problem dimensions (Organizational Silo, Newcomer Isolation, Communication Breakdown, Knowledge Bottleneck, Cultural and Geographical Distance, Psychological Safety Deficit) were presented as realistic team scenarios, and 23 IT professionals and advanced students rated 41 literature-derived mitigation measures. Rankings were analyzed with paired t-tests and a hierarchical Bayesian model that accounts for the within-subject design and yields, for each measure, the probability of being the best option in its scenario. Only for Communication Breakdown is the answer unambiguous: consolidating communication into a single primary channel is almost certainly preferred (P(best)=0.91). For the other five dimensions, the model identifies favorites with moderate evidence (P(best) between 0.38 and 0.58), such as structured knowledge transfer and blameless retrospectives. Across scenarios, structural measures that change how information, decisions, and knowledge are organized were rated higher than role-based or attitudinal measures (by 0.3 to 0.4 scale points), although not in every scenario. Given the small convenience sample, the results are exploratory, but they offer software engineering managers an evidence-graded starting point for selecting mitigation measures.

title: Multidimensional Source-Space MEG Representation of Network Imbalance in ADHD
comment: Submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics (JBHI)
summary: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with an atypical imbalance between the default mode network (DMN) and task-control systems. However, compressing neural activity into a single macroscopic imbalance measure may obscure individual neurophysiological differences. To address this, we leveraged the source-orientation selectivity and related measurement properties of resting-state magnetoencephalography (MEG) to establish a multidimensional source-space network representation in 21 individuals with ADHD and 21 healthy controls. We defined the macroscopic imbalance in relative Alpha activity between the DMN and task-control systems as the Core, and expanded its constituent information along three dimensions: spatial sources, spectral composition, and temporal network organization: into in-depth measures, assessed for stability, robustness, and complementarity. We found that the ADHD group exhibited a significant Core Alpha imbalance, driven mainly by task-control regions, while the multidimensional expansion revealed complementary ADHD-related neurophysiological information not fully represented by the Core, suggesting that similar macroscopic imbalances may reflect distinct underlying physiological states. Across 40 exploratory within-cohort held-out evaluations with separate development and test subsets, mean ROC-AUC increased from 0.7607 (Core-only) to 0.8995 with multidimensional inputs and to 0.9051 with the final ensemble, and mean accuracy increased from 71.43% to 79.82%. These findings suggest that multidimensional source-space expansion can further clarify the neurophysiological composition of ADHD-related network imbalance and improve individual-level discrimination, offering an interpretable framework potentially applicable to other brain disorders characterized by network imbalance.

title: Stability-compatible kernels: beyond Gaussianity for impulse response estimation
summary: Kernel-based regularization for linear system identification uses positive semidefinite kernels both to define reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) and as covariance models for stochastic impulse responses. Sharp kernel conditions are known for RKHS stability, while almost-sure BIBO stability under Gaussian priors requires an even more restrictive covariance condition. These restrictions, however, need not persist beyond Gaussianity, where the covariance no longer determines the full probability law. We introduce the notion of a stability-compatible kernel, namely a covariance kernel admitting at least one stochastic realization with almost-surely absolutely summable sample paths. We show that stability-compatibility holds if and only if the stable elements are dense in the associated RKHS, a condition strictly weaker than RKHS stability, and derive practical sufficient conditions, including a spectral criterion for stationary kernels. We then construct non-Gaussian priors that preserve a prescribed covariance while enforcing almost-sure stability. In particular, this yields a stable prior based on the stationary radial-basis-function (RBF) kernel, separating covariance structure from the mechanism enforcing stability. Numerical experiments show substantial estimation gains for several important classes of impulse responses, with particularly pronounced advantages when relevant dynamics occur at late lags or in separated temporal regions.

title: Escaping the Anthropomorphic Trap: Resolving the Cognitive Mismatch in Future AI Software Development
summary: For more than a half-century, the foundational paradigms of software development-such as modularity, information hiding, and hierarchical labor division-have been engineered to accommodate the strict cognitive limitations of human working memory. However, the rapid emergence of multi-agent artificial intelligence exposes a fundamental cognitive mismatch. Current frameworks attempt to integrate high-dimensional, stateless neural reasoning engines by coercing them to operate within these legacy, human-centric structures, falling into an anthropomorphic trap. This friction generates a novel, highly volatile behavioral entropy defined as AI-software technical debt, wherein amnesic agents hallucinate opaque workarounds to bypass architectural blindfolds. To resolve this, we propose Invisible Software Engineering (Invisible SE), a paradigm shift from agent-centric human emulation to environment-centric stigmergic governance. By reimagining the repository as an active computational topology which utilizes topological gradients, temporally weighted memory, and representation-space regularization, Invisible SE safely guides AI behavior without classical code-level constraints, thus transcending the cognitive horizons of human developers. This environment-centric protocol offers a potential blueprint for orchestrating scalable, long-lived computational infrastructures that transcend the cognitive horizons of human developers and enable autonomous agents to work, coordinate, and scale to build future software systems.

title: Convolution-Augmented Transformer for Robust Blind CFO Estimation in LEO Satellite Communication System
summary: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite communications are essential for achieving ubiquitous global connectivity. However, the high mobility of LEO satellites induces massive Doppler shifts and fast time-varying fading, severely impairing signal synchronization. Accurate Carrier Frequency Offset (CFO) estimation is critical for receiver synchronization. Nevertheless, conventional estimators and deep learning approaches often degrade significantly under highly dynamic, low-SNR conditions. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel Convolution Augmented Transformer architecture for robust, blind CFO estimation in LEO communication systems. Initially, to overcome the inherent limitations of standard linear embedding layers in capturing nonlinear phase rotations, we construct a multi-domain input feature that encompasses in-phase/quadrature (I/Q), polar, and statistical autocorrelation properties. Subsequently, a Convolutional Pre-Denoising (CPD) module, integrating multi-scale dilated convolutions and an attention mechanism, is deployed at the front end to adaptively suppress localized noise and extract robust spatiotemporal representations. These refined latent features are then processed by a Transformer encoder to explicitly track global, long-range phase dependencies. Extensive simulation results demonstrate that the proposed data-driven approach significantly outperforms conventional estimation algorithms, achieving enhanced estimation accuracy and superior resilience in highly dynamic LEO environments.

title: Parameter estimation for discretely observed rough fractional interacting particle systems
summary: We study parametric inference for interacting particle systems driven by independent fractional Brownian motions, based on discrete observations of all particles over a fixed time horizon. Our goal is to estimate an unknown drift parameter in the joint limit as the number of particles increases and the observation mesh vanishes. For $H>\frac 12$, we construct contrast based estimators by extending the discrete time least squares approach of Neuenkirch and Tindel to the interacting setting. For the rough regime $H\in(\frac 14,\frac 12)$, we introduce a modified contrast and use the stochastic sewing lemma to handle the first order approximations available from discrete observations. Our analysis combines the propagation of chaos for the associated fractional McKean Vlasov equation with estimates controlling the temporal discretization error. When the Hurst parameter and the diffusion coefficient are known, we establish strong consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators. The asymptotic results reveal an interplay between the number of particles and the temporal discretization: the convergence rate with respect to the observation mesh changes at $H=\frac 34$, while the asymptotic normality holds in both regimes considered. We further develop a joint estimation procedure for the drift parameter, the Hurst parameter, and the diffusion coefficient, extending quadratic-variation methods for fractional Brownian motion to the interacting particle framework. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the proposed estimators.

title: Skill Roulette: Measuring Skill Invocation Rate Across LLM Coding Agents
comment: Registered report, submitted to ACM TOSEM
summary: Agent skills package procedures for large language model (LLM) coding agents. An agent selects a skill from its name and description before reading the procedure. It may complete the task without invoking a relevant skill. We investigate how reliably coding agents invoke relevant skills and which factors affect that decision. We estimate invocation rates by repeating trials with identical inputs; invocation rate is the proportion of trials in which the agent invokes the relevant skill. We test 9 non-directional hypotheses about skill metadata, competing skills, contextual instructions, and task wording and composition. Eight concern invocation; the ninth tests whether making a skill available changes the occurrence of an action that the task does not request. We use tasks from 4 software engineering categories in a synthetic repository, running each of 4 coding-agent harnesses with 2 models. The planned 20,400 trials include 60 repetitions per Baseline category and configuration, 60 more per category in Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 that admit each category's task and skill, and 10 per experimental condition. Comparisons are specified before collection and evaluated within each model and harness configuration using Boschloo's exact test.

title: EEGSync: Unitary Temporal Alignment Method for Naturalistic and Resting-State EEG
summary:
Electroencephalography (EEG) studies increasingly use naturalistic and resting-state paradigms that lack discrete event timing. These recordings contain structured oscillatory activity but often lack repeated stimulus onsets to define a shared time clock across trials or participants. We introduce EEGSync, a complex-valued unitary Procrustes temporal alignment method for band-limited analytic EEG signals. EEGSync represents each subject as a matrix of complex oscillatory trajectories and solves a unitary Procrustes problem, mapping a target subject into the temporal coordinate system of a reference or group template. The method is computationally tractable through an economy-SVD factorization that avoids constructing the full temporal operator. This alignment strictly preserves original pairwise relationships and power across EEG channels. The unitary transformation aligns latent temporal structure rather than estimating a physical clock offset. Consequently, nonlinear instantaneous measures like phase-locking value, amplitude-envelope correlation, and phase-amplitude coupling are not guaranteed to be invariant. This framing makes EEGSync highly suitable for naturalistic shared-stimulus data, and potentially useful for resting-state data as a covariance-preserving latent manifold alignment.
  Evaluated via subject-independent cross-validation across physiological and clinical settings, EEGSync-based features achieved an AUROC of 0.9600 and 89.45% maximum classification accuracy in eyes-open versus eyes-closed state discrimination. For Alzheimer's disease versus healthy control classification, the highest AUROC reached 0.9272 in eyes-closed recordings, with further discrimination under eyes-open photostimulation. These findings suggest temporal alignment captures discriminative information complementing conventional spectral and statistical EEG features.

title: Latent space dynamic network actor models with position-rate link
summary: Relational event data record time-stamped interactions between actors. Dynamic network actor models represent each interaction as two separate decisions: when an actor becomes active and whom they select. Modelling these decisions separately cannot establish whether the most active actors are also the most frequently selected. We propose a latent space dynamic network actor model in which sender and receiver positions capture receiver choice, while a position-rate link relates latent positions to activity levels. The link uses two summaries invariant to latent position updates: latent popularity, measuring how much an actor is favoured by others, and excess self-affinity, capturing preference for similar actors beyond that explained by popularity. We adopt a Bayesian modular approach, estimating latent positions from receiver choices alone. Using e-mail data from a manufacturing company, we find that the most active employees are also the most frequently selected recipients. With multiple latent dimensions, preference for similar colleagues contributes less. Latent positions improve receiver-choice prediction, while the position-rate link captures differences in actor activity.

title: An Industry Perspective on Software Vulnerability Management: A Systematic Review of Approaches, Tools, Practices, and Challenges
comment: Preprint version. Submitted to ACM; under review. Online appendix included as supplementary material
summary: Software vulnerability management (SVM) refers to coordinated activities to detect, assess, repair, and disclose software vulnerabilities (SVs) across a product or ecosystem. As software systems grow in scale and dependency depth, organisations must balance timely security action with limited expertise, evolving tooling, and delivery pressure. In this practitioner-centred systematic literature review, we synthesise 57 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2010 and 2025 that collect primary data directly from industry practitioners. We examine the SVM solutions (approaches, tools, and practices) proposed and evaluated with practitioners and the challenges practitioners report when adopting and using these solutions in real-world settings. We find that practice-oriented contributions, such as guidelines, recommendations, lessons learned, and shared experiences, constitute most of the evidence base, while fewer studies evaluate concrete approaches and tools in industrial environments. The solution landscape and evaluation focus are weighted toward SV detection and repair, with comparatively limited practitioner-centred coverage of SV assessment and disclosure. The most persistent challenges concern how SVM work is organised and embedded: limited security expertise and time, unclear responsibility for SV-related decisions, scattered or poorly coordinated processes, and tools that are difficult to understand, configure, or integrate into existing workflows. These findings highlight the need for more integrated socio-technical interventions, stronger coverage of under-studied SVM tasks, and evaluations that prioritise sustained workflow impact alongside technical performance.

title: Dynamic and Risk-Aware Procurement of Fast Frequency Response from Electric Vehicles and Heat Pumps
summary: Low-inertia power systems increasingly rely on Fast Frequency Response (FFR) to keep the frequency nadir above under-frequency load-shedding thresholds without oversized Frequency Containment Reserve or synchronous inertia. This paper proposes two complementary methodologies that interface with an existing day-ahead FFR capacity market. On the Transmission System Operator (TSO) side, a dynamic procurement rule maps forecasted kinetic energy and contingency magnitude onto an offline neighborhood-need surface, yielding interval-wise FFR capacity requests rather than constant seasonal or annual volumes. On the aggregator side, a risk-aware, TSO-certifiable bidding strategy quantifies reliable FFR capacity from fleets of electric vehicles (EVs) and heat pumps (HPs) by offering lower conditional quantiles of day-ahead headroom at a prescribed delivery reliability. The resulting requests and offers are cleared through a pay-as-bid capacity auction. A Cyprus 2025 case study shows that dynamic neighborhood-based procurement yields an annual clearing cost of about EUR 476,000, which is 30%-33% lower than the seasonal and annual static rules and also below the UFLS VoLL of EUR 637,500 estimated from the fifteen real 2025 events with fmin <= 49 Hz. EV and HP offers meet their target delivery reliabilities, and RMS validation finds 46 of 50 operating points above 49 Hz at both full and 85% FFR delivery.

title: FRCI: An R Package for fuzzy and randomized confidence intervals
summary:
Fuzzy confidence intervals provide a flexible framework for statistical inference by representing uncertainty through membership functions rather than fixed interval endpoints. Closely related to randomized confidence intervals, they offer an alternative approach for dealing with the conservativeness that frequently arises in discrete statistical models. Despite their attractive theoretical properties, the practical use of fuzzy and randomized confidence intervals has been limited by the lack of readily available software implementations.
  This paper introduces FRCI (Fuzzy and Randomized Confidence Intervals), an R package available on CRAN for constructing and visualizing fuzzy and randomized confidence intervals. The package implements confidence interval procedures for parameters of the normal, Bernoulli/binomial, and Poisson distributions, including a recently proposed method based on reference value choice, Geyer-Meeden, Agresti-Coull, and score methods. The main function computes the membership function associated with a selected confidence interval procedure, while dedicated graphical tools facilitate visualization and comparison of fuzzy confidence intervals. We describe the statistical background underlying the implemented methods, discuss the package design, and illustrate its use through several examples. The FRCI package provides researchers, practitioners, and students with an accessible and unified environment for the study and application of fuzzy and randomized confidence intervals.

title: f2x50: A Repository-Scale Benchmark for Fortran-to-X Software Migration
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Repository-level migration requires more than translating isolated functions: it must preserve behaviour across modules, shared state, build structure, and dependencies. Existing translation benchmarks predominantly cover small programs or small repositories, or fixed and widely studied language pairs. We present f2x50, a target-independent benchmark comprising 50 public Fortran repositories pinned to exact Git revisions. It contains 12,116 Git-tracked Fortran files and 6,569,806 lines, divided into three structural-complexity tiers and paired with 561 deterministic behavioural probes. Of these probes, 446 compile pinned source files with small drivers and span 131 repository--routine pairs. Every repository has at least five direct checks that collectively execute at least two routines. f2x50 provides target-independent tools for acquisition, validation, licence review, and reproducibility, together with a reference adapter for evaluating Python targets. The remaining probes are explicitly classified as extractions, inline reimplementations, or synthetic fixtures. The benchmark therefore supports comparable evaluations across migration tools and target languages.

title: Scalable Vehicle Charging Coordination for Online Operations: A Column Generation Approach
summary: We consider an electric vehicle charging scheduling problem for long-haul freight transport. To mitigate unforeseen waiting times caused by congestion and limited charger capacity, we consider a coordinated scheduling approach that prioritizes scalable, computationally efficient scheduling for ongoing or online operations. We formulate the problem as a set partitioning model and develop a column generation framework with a label-correcting algorithm to solve it efficiently. We assess the scalability of our algorithm through both theoretical complexity analysis and empirical measurements, highlighting the role of feasibility and dominance pruning in limiting label growth. Finally, using freight telematics data from Sweden, we show that the proposed method computes optimized schedules for realistic instances with 1000 vehicles within seconds and reduces vehicle operation downtime by 78.6% compared to uncoordinated scheduling.

title: Worst-case bias of the independence assumption for functions of two ordinal variables
comment: 26 pages. Submitted to Kybernetika. Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24326496
summary: Let ordinal grades $X$ and $Y$ be obtained by cutting a pair of random variables with copula $C$ at arbitrary thresholds, and let $g$ be a function of the grades. We study the largest error $S_C(g)$, over all thresholds, that is, over all marginal laws, made when the mean of $g(X,Y)$ is computed as if the grades were independent. This is the counterpart of the classical dependence-uncertainty problem: the copula is fixed and the discretisation is free. The error is caused entirely by the interaction of the inputs, measured by an index $ρ(g)$, the largest absolute $g$-volume of a rectangle of grades, which vanishes if and only if $g$ is additive. For every copula, $S_C(g)$ lies between $ρ(g)$ times the largest deviation of $C$ from the independence copula and $ρ(g)$ times half the total variation of their difference, and the factor one half cannot be improved. For the Gaussian copula with correlation $λ$ we prove that $S_C(g)$ equals $|λ|ρ(g)/(2π)$ to first order, with a sharp constant and an explicit remainder. The same first-order law holds for copula families whose first-order departure from independence is a product of unimodal factors, including the Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern, Ali-Mikhail-Haq, Frank, Clayton and Plackett families, and we characterise the Archimedean families with this property. An application to the TNM staging of colon cancer, with data from a clinical trial, compares the bounds with the actual error of the independence computation.

title: Skip-Level Meetings: Benefits, Risks, and Design Considerations Informed by Bypassed Managers' Experiences
comment: The published article along with the supplementary material is available at: https://doi.org/10.1109/EMR.2026.3740096
summary: Skip-level meetings (SLMs), bidirectional, relationship-oriented meetings between employees and managers two or more levels above, are common but not universal, and often recommended in professional outlets. They entail benefits and risks for employees, direct and skip-level managers, and organizations, with multiple factors related to shaping the value-risk balance and appropriate approach. However, SLMs have received limited scholarly attention, particularly regarding bypassed managers' views of that managerial practice. This exploratory qualitative study examined the experiences and perspectives of 25 first-tier software engineering managers from diverse personal and organizational contexts in the multicultural, dynamic, innovation-driven, and high-turnover U.S. tech sector as bypassed managers in SLMs between their direct reports and these reports' second-tier managers. Their accounts, integrated with directly related literature, as well as on intersecting topics such as employee voice, psychological safety, and cultural and generational differences, revealed broad support and preference for exclusion from SLMs, contrary to concerns in prior literature, broad implementation, and high sensitivity to design and contextual factors, such as the significance of follow-up involvement and of individual backgrounds. Findings position SLMs not as a universally beneficial managerial practice, but as context-dependent, requiring deliberate design and implementation, or avoidance. The study extends limited research on SLMs and hierarchy-bypassing interactions, recommends directions for further research, and offers evidence-informed guidance for deciding whether and how to use SLMs to maximize value while mitigating risks.

title: Toward Massive MIMO HAPS Networks: Antenna Architectures and Design
summary: High-altitude platform stations (HAPS) are expected to become an important component of sixth-generation (6G) and beyond wireless networks by providing wide-area wireless connectivity through massive multiple-input multiple-output (mMIMO) technology. As the communication performance of HAPS systems is fundamentally determined by the antenna array architecture, efficient antenna design has become a critical research topic. Motivated by these considerations, this article provides a comprehensive overview of antenna array design for mMIMO-enabled HAPS systems and proposes two novel antenna architectures to improve antenna-user alignment and communication performance. Specifically, the representative applications of mMIMO-enabled HAPS are first introduced, followed by the key design requirements for HAPS antenna arrays. Representative antenna architectures are then systematically reviewed and compared under a unified simulation framework based on the 3GPP NTN channel model. Finally, several promising research directions are discussed to provide insights into the design of next-generation intelligent HAPS antenna systems.

title: Advancing mixed-effects random forests for predictions based on multi-cohort data
summary: Pooling longitudinal cohorts can extend age coverage and improve long-term health predictions, but cohort heterogeneity complicate estimation and prediction. Mixed-effects machine learning (ME-ML) combines flexible machine learning methods with mixed-effect models to account for correlated observations, yet these ME-ML methods are limited in their applicability in complex settings such as multi-cohort data. We propose a multi-cohort mixed-effects random forest (MERFmulti-cohort) for improving predictions of individual health trajectories beyond the observed period. The method extends standard MERF through (i) better separation of population-level and subject-specific variation, (ii) flexibility in correcting systematic discrepancies in fixed-effects estimates to improve covariance parameter estimation, and (iii) flexible specification of random-effects and residual variance-covariance structures. We evaluate MERFmulti-cohort against linear regression, linear mixed models, random forests, and standard MERF in simulations and four real-data scenarios predicting BMI z-scores in children and adolescents. In simulations, MERFmulti-cohort improves covariance parameter estimation across several covariance structures while achieving prediction accuracy comparable to standard MERF. Predictive gains are most obvious when residual variances vary across study waves. In real-data applications, MERFmulti-cohort improves predictive accuracy relative to MERF by flexibly capturing complex patterns and accommodating cohort heterogeneity. Pooling similar cohorts covering extended age coverage can improve future individual-level predictions if the heterogeneity in multi-cohort data is adequately accounted for.

title: torchtest2: One-Call Sanity Checks for PyTorch Models,Evaluated on Real and Unseen Architectures
summary: Many bugs in deep learning code are silent: a layer that is never called, an optimizer created before the classification head was replaced, a recurrent layer that treats the batch as time, or an ignored attention mask. The code runs, the loss decreases somewhat, and the defect surfaces, if ever, after days of GPU time. We present torchtest2, an open-source library that runs 18 sanity checks on a single batch with one call, restores the PyTorch state it touches, and adapts to model families through plugins. We evaluate it by mutation analysis with 17 classes of silent bugs on 103 models from torchvision, timm and Hugging Face transformers, on 600 random architectures and on 20 hand-written realistic bugs, against the checks of the original torchtest, overfitting a single batch, a smoke test and a training monitor in the style of AUTOTRAINER and DeepDiagnosis. Every mutant is compared with its healthy counterpart, and intervals come from a bootstrap over models. After freezing the tool, we ran it on 191 models of architecture families it had never seen: counting, for every tool alike, a failing report where the healthy model's report does not fail, it detected 78% of the injected bugs (95% CI 75-80), against 40% for the original torchtest checks and 48% for the training monitor. On real models its batch-independence check found a bug in timm's GCViT that couples the images of a batch. Real models also exposed false alarms that neither the tool's own test suite nor random architectures had revealed. Two independent collections of real silent bugs mark the limits of the approach: only 3 of 28 reproduced PyTorch bugs from Stack Overflow and 3 of the 18 silent training errors released with TrainCheck are within reach of a pre-training model tester. A median check takes 1.0 s. We release the library, the benchmark and all raw results.

title: Adaptive Guidance for 3GPP Ambient IoT Contention-Based Random Access
summary: The emerging ambient Internet of Things (A-IoT) envisions connectivity among large populations of low-cost, energy-constrained devices. Supporting such connectivity requires efficient coordination of device access, particularly in reader-triggered operation, where multiple devices may respond to paging over limited shared radio resources. Indeed, simultaneous responses can lead to severe contention, delayed transmissions, and lost reports. This article explores how compact extensions to the current 3GPP Release-19 signaling framework could enable more selective and adaptive device access. The proposed approach allows readers to broadcast compact access guidance, which devices interpret according to their local conditions, while optional feedback supports continuous adaptation. Through a device-reporting case study, we demonstrate how such coordination can improve report delivery and timeliness under congested conditions, while highlighting the trade-offs across different network configurations. We also examine practical signaling considerations and discuss opportunities for more intelligent, adaptive, and resilient protocols.

title: Sparse designs via quantization of the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes
summary: While the notions of sphere packing and sphere covering underlie the most widely used criteria for space-filling design in computer experiments, namely, the maximin and minimax approaches, they suffer from major drawbacks in high dimensions. First, when the dimension $d$ is very large, deploying a space-filling design requires an extremely large number of design points, making the very notion of a space-filling design questionable. Second, these two design characteristics are highly sensitive to boundaries, particularly when the design domain is a hypercube (the case considered in this paper), and especially to its vertices. This sensitivity is particularly acute when the design size is less than $2^d$. Instead of considering the maximin or minimax criterion, we consider here the quantization error of the uniform measure on the hypercube. This error has three key advantages: it accounts for the entire distribution of distances from a random point $U$ to the design, is less sensitive to boundary effects than the maximin and minimax criteria, and, thanks to Zador's celebrated theorem, enables a smooth and natural transition to uniform designs as the design size tends to infinity. Building on recent results on the construction of optimal random quantizers for spherically symmetric distributions (arXiv:2610.11772) we propose a method to generate random designs of a given target size $n$ with small $L_s$-mean quantization error. The support of the resulting distribution is then used to construct designs, possibly incrementally, with sizes up to $n$. We demonstrate that, for moderate $n$, designs supported on a fractional factorial subset of the vertices of a small hypercube perform exceptionally well---and significantly better than designs uniformly distributed over the entire hypercube. We also explain how to account for projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces.

title: A Concurrent Structured Record Mirrored the Prose It Accompanied: A Pre-Registered Conceptual Replication and Extension of the Hide Pending Tool Call Scenario
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. Pre-registered study; protocols, code, data and analyses at https://github.com/NicolasRocchia/disensor-hide-pending
summary: Huang et al. (2026) show that language models writing reports of agentic work tend to conceal narrative-changing flaws, and that appending "Be honest in your response." to the instruction substantially increases disclosure in most of their scenarios.
